title: Archiving and compression
lead: Bundle files with tar, gzip and zip, compress them, restore them safely and verify your backups.
objectives: You explain the difference between archiving (tar: bundling) and compression (gzip, bzip2, xz).
You create archives with `tar -czf`, list them with `tar -tf` and extract into a new directory with `tar -xzf -C`.
You know the risks of tar bombs and overwriting, and always list before extracting.
You use `gzip -k` and `zip`/`unzip` and compare compression ratios.
You make a dated backup and verify it with `sha256sum`.

sections.title: Archiving and compression are different things
body: **Archiving** means **bundling** many files and directories, with their paths and permissions, into **one** file; the size does not shrink. `tar` (tape archive) does this. **Compression** shrinks a single file: `gzip` (fast, common), `bzip2` (smaller, slower), `xz` (smallest, slowest).
In practice you use both: `tar` bundles, then gzip compresses. The result is a `.tar.gz` or `.tgz` file. `tar` does both in one command with `-z` (gzip), `-j` (bzip2) or `-J` (xz).
Important detail: `gzip notes.txt` **deletes** the original file and leaves only the `.gz` file. Use `-k` (keep) to preserve the original.

commands.what: Compresses a file and keeps the original (adds `.gz`).
commands.where: For large logs or text files.
commands.why: Without `-k` the original is deleted; with `-k` you can experiment safely.

commands.what: Decompresses a `.gz` file and deletes the `.gz` file (same as `gzip -d`).
commands.where: When you restore a single compressed file.
commands.why: `gunzip -k` keeps the `.gz` as a safety copy.

commands.what: Prints the content of a compressed file without decompressing it on disk.
commands.where: When reading old compressed logs or searching them with `grep`.
commands.why: No disk space or extra time spent on unpacking.

sections.tip: Compare sizes with `ls -lh`. Text and logs compress very well; already compressed JPG, MP4 or ZIP files barely shrink.
sections.warn: `gzip notes.txt` deletes the original. Back up data that exists only once first, or use `-k`.

sections.title: tar: create, list, extract
body: `tar` options can be combined in one word: **c** (create), **x** (extract), **t** (list), **v** (verbose), **f** (file, the archive name; **always the last letter**, the name follows immediately), **z/j/J** (gzip/bzip2/xz).
Always add **relative paths** to an archive (`project`, not `/home/student/project`). GNU tar strips a leading `/` and warns, so extracting cannot overwrite system files.
`-C directory` makes tar change into that directory first: when extracting it is the destination, when creating it is the root of the source. The target directory must already exist.

commands.what: Bundles a directory into one gzip-compressed archive.
commands.where: When making backups and before sending a project.
commands.why: One file is much easier to copy, transfer and store.

commands.what: Lists the paths inside the archive without extracting (`-z` not needed, tar detects the type).
commands.where: Before extracting, to see the content.
commands.why: Prevents tar bombs and overwrite surprises.

commands.what: Extracts the archive into the given (existing) directory.
commands.where: When restoring, to keep the current directory clean.
commands.why: Always extract into a new, empty directory, then check.

commands.what: Extracts only the named file or directory from the archive.
commands.where: When rescuing a single file from a backup.
commands.why: You do not extract everything or overwrite current files. The path must be written as in the `tar -tf` output.

commands.what: Leaves files matching the pattern out of the archive.
commands.where: To keep logs, temporary files or `.git` out of a backup.
commands.why: The backup gets smaller and faster. Put `--exclude` before the path to archive.

commands.what: Creates an archive with xz compression, the strongest level (`-j` is for bzip2).
commands.where: For archives that are rarely used and kept long.
commands.why: Smaller file, but slower and more CPU load.

sections.tip: Mnemonic: **c**reate, e**x**tract, lis**t**; then `f` and the file name. tar detects the compression type itself when extracting, so `tar -xf` is often enough.
sections.warn: The archive name must directly follow `f`. With `tar -cfz backup.tgz project`, `z` is taken as the archive name and the file ends up wrongly named.

sections.title: Extracting safely: tar bombs and overwriting
body: Some archives have no top-level directory; extracting dumps hundreds of files straight into your current directory (a **tar bomb**). Cleaning up is painful because you cannot tell which files came from the archive. Solution: list first with `tar -tf` (or `tar -tvf`), then extract into a new, empty directory.
`tar -x` **silently overwrites** existing files with the same name. Never extract directly into your working directory.

Permissions and owners: `tar` stores permissions in the archive. As **root**, owners and permissions are restored faithfully; as a normal user the `umask` applies. Use `-p` to explicitly preserve permissions. Restoring files owned by another user requires `sudo`.

commands.what: Lists the archive verbosely: permissions, owner, size, date and path.
commands.where: Before extracting, to check permissions and whether there is a top-level directory.
commands.why: You spot tar bombs and absolute paths in advance.

commands.what: Extracts the archive and preserves file permissions.
Extracts as root; owner and group are restored too.
commands.where: For system backups or files belonging to other users.
commands.why: Ownership is kept, but root also magnifies mistakes.

sections.tip: Habit: look with `tar -tf backup.tar.gz | head`, run `mkdir restore`, then `tar -xzf backup.tar.gz -C restore`.
sections.danger: Never extract an archive you do not trust as root, least of all with target `/` (`-C /`). Members with absolute paths or `..` can overwrite system files. Snapshot first, list first.

sections.title: zip and unzip
body: `zip` bundles and compresses at once and is compatible with Windows/macOS; ideal for exchanging files. Directories need `-r` (recursive). Install with `sudo apt install zip unzip` on Ubuntu or `sudo dnf install zip unzip` on Rocky/Alma.

Difference from `.tar.gz`: zip compresses each file separately, so extracting single files is fast; but it preserves Linux permissions and owners less reliably than `tar`. For Linux backups prefer `tar`.

commands.what: Adds a directory with its subdirectories to a zip archive.
commands.where: When sending files to Windows/macOS users.
commands.why: Opens everywhere; without `-r` the directory content is not added.

commands.what: Lists the content of a zip archive without extracting.
Extracts the zip archive into the given directory (created if needed).
commands.why: You do not scatter files into the current directory.

sections.title: A simple backup and verification
body: A simple backup: a name with the date, one command to bundle, plus a checksum. `date +%F` prints today as `2026-11-12`, so each backup gets its own name and never overwrites an older one. `$(...)` inside the command runs first and its output becomes part of the name.

`sha256sum` produces a file's fingerprint. If you check the backup with `sha256sum -c` after copying it, you know it is intact. A backup only counts once a copy lives **on another disk or machine**; also try a restore once.
Automatic backups use a scheduler (`cron` or a systemd timer). That is a topic for another module; here we run the command by hand.

commands.what: Prints the SHA-256 checksum of a file.
commands.where: When verifying backups or downloaded files.
commands.why: Even one changed bit changes the sum, so corruption shows up.

commands.what: Compares stored sums with the files; prints `OK` or `FAILED`.
commands.where: After copying a backup or before restoring it.
commands.why: You find a broken backup right away, not in a crisis.

commands.what: Creates a backup archive with today's date in its name.
commands.why: Old backups are not overwritten and versions stay distinguishable.

commands.where: For date stamps in file names.
commands.why: Produces names that sort by date.

sections.tip: The 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 different media, 1 off-site.

t01.text: You are in the `lab` directory. Look at the project tree to archive with `ls -R project`.
t01.hint: -R is uppercase; it lists subdirectories too.

t02.text: Create the `backups` directory for the backups: `mkdir backups`.

t03.text: Bundle `project` with gzip into the archive `backups/project.tar.gz` (`tar -czf ...`). The simulator does not run `tar`; the command's correctness is checked.

t04.text: List the archive's content without extracting: `tar -tzf backups/project.tar.gz`.

t05.text: Create the `restore` directory, then extract the archive there with `-C`: `tar -xzf backups/project.tar.gz -C restore`.
t05.hint: `mkdir restore` first; the `-C` target must exist.

t06.text: Compress `logs/app.log` and keep the original: `gzip -k logs/app.log`.
t06.hint: `-k` = keep. Without it the original is deleted.

t07.text: Extract only `project/notes.txt` from the archive into `restore`.
t07.hint: The member name goes at the end of the command, as shown by `tar -tf`: `project/notes.txt`.

t08.text: Predict: what total line count does `wc -l logs/*.log` show? Guess first, then run it.
t08.hint: Three files: `app.log`, `web.log`, `db.log`; the last line is `total`.

t09.text: Predict: which two paths does `find project -name '*.c' | sort` print? Run it to verify.
t09.hint: The paths start with `project/src/...` and are sorted alphabetically.

t10.text: Bundle the whole `lab` directory without the `.log` files into `backups/lab-nologs.tar.gz` (`--exclude='*.log'`).
t10.hint: Put the pattern in quotes and before the source path (`.`).

t11.text: Make a backup of `project` with today's date in the name: `backups/project-$(date +%F).tar.gz`.
t11.hint: `$(date +%F)` is command substitution; you can use it inside the name.

t12.text: Debug: a tar bomb dumped `bomb1.txt`, `bomb2.txt`, `bomb3.txt` into `lab`. Create a directory `cleanup` and move all three there.
t12.hint: `mkdir cleanup`, then `mv bomb1.txt bomb2.txt bomb3.txt cleanup/`.

t13.text: Mini project: create `staging`, copy the `project` tree into it with `cp -r`, check with `ls -R staging`, then bundle `staging` as `staging.tar.gz`.
t13.hint: Steps: `mkdir staging`, `cp -r project staging/`, `ls -R staging`, `tar -czf staging.tar.gz staging`.

t14.text: Challenge: add `project` recursively to `backups/project.zip` (`zip -r`), list it with `unzip -l`, then create its sum with `sha256sum`. All three in this order.

t15.text: TICKET #3801 — The auditors want compressed copies of the logs, but the originals in `logs` must stay. Create `audit`, copy `logs/*.log` into it and compress the copies with `gzip`.
t15.hint: `mkdir audit`, `cp logs/*.log audit/`, `gzip audit/*.log`; `gzip` only deletes the copies.

t16.text: Predict: what does `ls -1 project/src | wc -l` print? Run it to verify.

vm.intro: Run the commands below on your own VM (Ubuntu/Rocky/Alma). Everything stays in `~/lab`; your real data is untouched. No step is destructive, but archives overwrite files of the same name: do not experiment outside lab. Taking a snapshot before bigger experiments is a good habit.

v01.title: Set up the test project
v01.text: Create a small project and a big log file under `~/lab`, then list the project files.

blocks.cmd:
mkdir -p ~/lab/project/{src,docs}
cd ~/lab
echo 'int main(void) { return 0; }' > project/src/main.c
echo 'Demo project' > project/docs/readme.txt
echo 'todo: backup' > project/notes.txt
seq 1 200000 > big.log
find project -type f | sort

differs: The order may differ; all three files showing up is enough.
If `seq` is missing (very rare), use `yes line | head -n 200000 > big.log`.

v02.title: Archive and list without extracting
v02.text: Pack `project` into `backup.tar.gz`, list its content without extracting and check the size.

blocks.cmd:
cd ~/lab
tar -czf backup.tar.gz project
tar -tzf backup.tar.gz
ls -lh backup.tar.gz
blocks.expected:
project/
project/docs/
project/docs/readme.txt
project/notes.txt
project/src/
project/src/main.c
-rw-r--r--. 1 student student 300 Nov 12 10:00 backup.tar.gz

differs: The order of the list may differ.
Size and date differ; what matters is that paths start with `project/`.
The warning `Removing leading '/'` appears with absolute paths; it should not appear here.

v03.title: Restore safely
v03.text: Extract the archive into a new directory, then extract only a single file.

blocks.cmd:
cd ~/lab
mkdir restore restore2
tar -xzf backup.tar.gz -C restore
tar -xzf backup.tar.gz -C restore2 project/notes.txt
ls -R restore restore2
blocks.expected:
restore:
project
...
restore2:
project

restore2/project:
notes.txt

differs: If you see `Cannot open: No such file or directory`, the `-C` directory is missing; create it with `mkdir` first.
If tar says `Not found in archive`, write the path as shown by `tar -tf`.

v04.title: Compare compression ratios
v04.text: Compress `big.log` with gzip, bzip2 and xz, keeping the original. Compare the sizes.

blocks.cmd:
cd ~/lab
gzip -k big.log
bzip2 -k big.log
xz -k big.log
ls -l big.log*
blocks.expected:
-rw-r--r--. 1 student student 1228895 Nov 12 10:01 big.log
-rw-r--r--. 1 student student  580000 Nov 12 10:01 big.log.bz2
-rw-r--r--. 1 student student  480000 Nov 12 10:01 big.log.gz
-rw-r--r--. 1 student student  400000 Nov 12 10:01 big.log.xz

differs: If you get `bzip2: command not found`, install it: Ubuntu `sudo apt install bzip2`, Rocky/Alma `sudo dnf install bzip2`.
If an old `gzip` does not know `-k`, make a copy first with `cp big.log big2.log`.

v05.title: Dated backup and checksum
v05.text: Make a dated backup, save its checksum and verify it. Optionally try zip.

blocks.cmd:
cd ~/lab
tar -czf backup-$(date +%F).tar.gz project
sha256sum backup-*.tar.gz > SHA256SUMS
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS

# Optional (without zip: sudo apt install zip unzip or sudo dnf install zip unzip)
zip -r project.zip project
unzip -l project.zip

differs: If you see `FAILED`, you changed the archive after computing the sum; run `sha256sum` again.
On a German or Turkish system the output may be translated instead of `OK`.
If `backup-*.tar.gz` matches several files, you get one line for each.

q1.q: Which command only lists an archive's content without extracting?

q2.explain: gzip replaces the original with the compressed file. Use `gzip -k` to keep it.

q3.q: Why do you list an archive with `tar -tf` before extracting?
options: To see tar bombs and files that would be overwritten beforehand
Because `tar -x` does not work without listing
q3.explain: Without a top-level directory the files scatter into the current directory, and existing files can be overwritten.

q4.q: What does `-C restore` do in `tar -xzf backup.tar.gz -C restore`?
options: Compresses the archive under the name `restore`
Changes into `restore` before extracting and extracts there
q4.explain: `-C` (change directory) sets the target directory; it must exist beforehand.

summary: Archiving (`tar`) bundles, compression (`gzip`, `bzip2`, `xz`) shrinks; `.tar.gz` is the combination.
Create: `tar -czf backup.tar.gz project`; list: `tar -tf`; extract: `tar -xzf ... -C restore`.
List first, then extract into a new directory: protects against tar bombs and overwriting.
`gzip` deletes the original, `gzip -k` keeps it; zip is compatible with Windows/macOS.
Make dated backups, verify them with `sha256sum` and test a restore.

glossary.meaning: Many files and directories, with their paths, bundled into one file (`tar`).
An archive without a top-level directory that scatters files into the current directory when extracted.
Absolute paths start with `/`; relative paths are preferred inside archives.
A file's fingerprint (`sha256sum`); makes corruption visible.
